01.r: No person at all is to be left owed.
01.n: Greek piles up negatives for emphasis: literally 'to no one nothing owe'. English uses one negative, 'no one anything'. Abbott-Smith cites this verse under the word, with the meanings no, none, no one, and in the neuter, nothing.

03.r: A command: let no debt stand unpaid.
03.n: The present form can be read as a statement ('you owe') or a command ('owe'); all six translations, and this study, take it as a command. The present tense suggests an ongoing state: do not stay in anyone's debt.

04.r: With μή, 'if not': the one exception to the rule.
04.n: εἰ μή is literally 'if not'; together the two words mean 'except'.

05.r: The negative in 'if not', that is, 'except'.

06.r: The article makes 'to love one another' into a noun phrase: the loving of one another.
06.n: Greek can put an article before an infinitive; English has no equivalent, and 'to love' carries both words.

07.r: Love that runs both ways among the readers.

08.r: The one thing they are to go on owing each other.
08.n: Abbott-Smith gives the sense 'to feel and exhibit esteem and goodwill to a person'. A present infinitive: love as an ongoing obligation. That this debt can never be fully paid off is a reasonable reading of the verse, but it is an inference.

09.r: The article turns the participle 'loving' into a person: the one who loves.

10.r: Gives the reason for the command.

11.r: A present participle: the one who goes on loving.

12.r: With 'other', marks the other person in any relationship.

13.r: The other person, whoever he is.
13.n: Literally 'the other'. The DRC, ASV and BSB render it 'neighbour', which is the sense, but not the word: Abbott-Smith's entry for 'love' shows the usual Greek word for neighbour, πλησίον, in another verse. Abbott-Smith notes that this word properly means the second of two.

14.r: The law of God given to Israel, by the most natural reading.
14.n: There is no article in the Greek; the YLT shows this with plain 'law'. Abbott-Smith derives the word from νέμω, to deal out or distribute.

15.r: The one who loves has done all the law requires.
15.n: The perfect tense: the fulfilment is complete and stands. Abbott-Smith's first sense of the verb is to fill or make full.

tr_note: The Textus Receptus has ἀλλήλους, 'one another', in a different position in the phrase. The meaning is the same, which is why the KJV reads 'to love one another' as we do.
